card.name: Bunny hop
card.tagline: A 1952 novelty dance from San Francisco involving a conga-style line and rhythmic hops.
card.profile: The Bunny Hop is a social novelty dance originating from Balboa High School in San Francisco in 1952. Performed in a line or open circle, participants hold the hips of the person in front, executing a rhythmic sequence of taps and hops. The dance is traditionally set to Ray Anthony’s big band composition, though it has been adapted to various musical styles including mambo and salsa. It remains a living tradition, appearing in popular media and regional variations like the Finnish letkajenkka and the Saudi Arabian 'penguin dance.'
card.insight: Created at Balboa High School in 1952, the Bunny Hop evolved from a local novelty into a global phenomenon, appearing as the Finnish 'letkajenkka' and the Saudi Arabian 'penguin dance' (raqsat al-batriq).

card.profile_long:
The Bunny Hop emerged in 1952 within the hallways of Balboa High School in San Francisco. As a novelty dance, it quickly transcended its school origins to become a fixture of American social dance, largely propelled by the big band recording of Ray Anthony. The dance is fundamentally a variation of the conga line, characterized by a specific, repetitive sequence of footwork performed while connected to others in a chain. Participants form a line or an open circle, each person placing their hands on the hips of the individual directly in front of them. This physical connection creates a unified, moving structure led by the person at the front of the line, who guides the group across the dance floor.

The movement sequence consists of a rhythmic pattern: tapping the floor twice with the right foot, followed by two taps with the left foot. This is immediately followed by a series of hops: one forward, one backward, and three forward. This sequence repeats throughout the duration of the musical track. The simplicity of this structure allowed it to be easily adopted and adapted across different cultures and decades. In Finland, the dance is known as the 'letkajenkka,' which utilizes essentially the same steps. In 2014, the dance gained significant popularity in Saudi Arabia, where it was performed to different music and referred to as 'raqsat al-batriq' or the 'penguin dance,' becoming a staple at wedding celebrations.

Musically, the dance is most closely associated with Ray Anthony’s 1952 vocal hit and his 1953 instrumental re-recording. However, the versatility of the rhythm has allowed for diverse interpretations. Duke Ellington famously recorded a 'Bunny Hop Mambo' in 1954, and other artists such as The Applejacks and The Champs have also recorded versions of the tune. The dance has maintained a persistent presence in popular culture, appearing in television programs such as 'Family Ties,' 'The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air,' 'Everybody Loves Raymond,' and 'Newhart,' as well as in the film 'Cry-Baby' and 'The Addams Family Musical.' Its longevity is marked by its ability to be performed in various social settings, from high school gymnasiums to wedding receptions and even, as noted in a 1979 police report, in public spaces. Despite its lighthearted nature, the dance remains a recognizable, living tradition that continues to be performed and adapted globally.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance was created in 1952 at Balboa High School in San Francisco. It gained national attention through Ray Anthony's big band recordings in 1952 and 1953.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Participants form a line or circle, holding the hips of the person in front. The sequence involves two taps with the right foot, two taps with the left, one hop forward, one hop backward, and three hops forward.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is traditionally performed to big band music, specifically Ray Anthony's eponymous composition. Other versions include mambo and salsa arrangements.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is a social novelty dance used at weddings, parties, and social events. It has been used in popular culture to signify lighthearted or nostalgic social interaction.
sections.lineage: A variation on the conga line.

claims.text: The bunny hop is a novelty dance created at Balboa High School in San Francisco in 1952.
Ray Anthony co-wrote and recorded an eponymous song in 1952 and an instrumental in 1953.
The dance is a variation on a conga line.
Participants dance in a line or a circle, holding on to the hips of the person in front of them.
They tap the floor two times with their right foot, then with their left foot, then they hop forwards, backwards, and finally three hops forward to finish the sequence
The letkajenkka from Finland has essentially the same steps.
In 2014 in Saudi Arabia, the same dance set to slightly different music (referred to as 'raqsat al-batriq', the 'penguin dance') became a popular trend
